BPM Justification: Forcing sustainability onto the same decision table as time/cost/quality/flexibility is exactly the kind of structural change that gets environmental impact taken seriously instead of traded away first - this is as close to a lever as strategy-level guidance gets.

A six-area capability checklist is a sound planning discipline, but from a sustainability-outcomes point of view it's a generic 'don't forget these dimensions' management checklist that happens to be phrased in BPM's own vocabulary rather than a mechanism with direct environmental effect.

Unordered, ad hoc work is exactly where a lot of real-world environmental waste hides precisely because nobody's measuring it, so widening the net beyond formally modeled processes matters a lot even though the chapter doesn't hand you a concrete technique for it.

Putting environmental indicators in the same scorecard executives already watch is one of the highest-leverage adoption moves there is - metrics that live next to revenue and customer numbers get acted on in a way a standalone sustainability report never does.

Activity-level emissions data is precisely the granularity needed to find real reduction opportunities instead of vague process-level estimates, and the case studies back it with two concrete sectors (public shared services, airport operations).
A maturity model gives organizations a staged path rather than an all-or-nothing ask, which is usually what actually gets sustainability initiatives funded and sustained past the first pilot.

Sustainability data that only shows up once a year in a corporate report never changes day-to-day behavior; pushing it into the same dynamic indicator systems that already drive operational decisions is the difference between reporting and managing.

Real-time energy data is only actionable if it reaches the same dashboards and event systems that already drive operational response - bolting it onto facilities reporting instead would mean nobody acts on it in time to matter.

Projects are where strategy actually gets implemented, so if sustainability isn't a selection/success criterion at the project gate, it never survives contact with a real budget and timeline - this is a genuinely high-leverage intervention point.

Shared environmental-data platforms are valuable for scope-3-style supply-chain visibility, but the chapter's contribution is a general data-sharing network architecture that would be just as applicable outside any BPM context.
